source_refs.note: Book p. 52-53: 2.10.2 definition, global extrema, Example (a)-(c) with Figures 2.2-2.4, local maxima/minima table, Figure 2.5

blocks.text: Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) has a global (absolute) minimum at \(x = c \in I\), if \(f(c) \le f(x)\) for all \(x \in I\).
If \(f(x)\) has a global (absolute) minimum at \(x = c\), then \(f(c)\) is called global (absolute) minimum value of the function.
The global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively called its global extrema.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the definition of 2.10.1 with the inequality reversed: now \(f(c)\) is never larger than any other value. "Extrema" is the plural of "extremum"; it covers both maxima and minima.

blocks.title: Example (a)
blocks.problem: Let \(f(x) = x^{2}\) be defined on the interval \([0, 2]\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) on \([0, 2]\).
To find: the global maximum and global minimum.
Method: \(f'(x) = 2x \ge 0\) on \([0, 2]\), so \(f\) is increasing there (2.9): its smallest value is at the left end and its largest at the right end.

The function \(f\) has a global maximum at \(x = 2\) and a global minimum at \(x = 0\). The corresponding maximum and minimum values of the function are:
\[f(2) = 4 \text{ (global maximum value)}\]
\[f(0) = 0 \text{ (global minimum value)}\]
(See Figure 2.2.)
Why: for \(0 \le x \le 2\) we have \(0 \le x^{2} \le 4\), so \(f(0) \le f(x) \le f(2)\) for every \(x\) in the interval.
Check: \(f(1) = 1\) and \(f(1.5) = 2.25\) both lie between 0 and 4.
blocks.answer: Global maximum value \(f(2) = 4\); global minimum value \(f(0) = 0\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel: axes with ticks 1 and 2 on the x-axis and 1 to 4 on the y-axis. The curve f(x) = x squared runs from the origin, labelled f(0) = 0, up to the dot (2, 4), labelled f(2) = 4. A dashed red line drops from (2, 4) to the x-axis and a dot marks 4 on the y-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.2: f(x) = x² on [0, 2] (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example (b)
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
To find: its absolute extrema.
Method: compare \(f(x)\) with \(f(0)\) using \(x^{2} \ge 0\).

\[f(x) = x^{2} \ge 0 = f(0)\]
So \(f\) has an absolute minimum value at \(x = 0\), where \(f(0) = 0\). (See Figure 2.3.)
Why: a square is never negative.

It has no absolute maximum value.
Why: for any number \(M\), taking \(x = \sqrt{|M|} + 1\) gives \(x^{2} > M\): the values grow without bound.
blocks.answer: Absolute minimum value \(f(0) = 0\); no absolute maximum.

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel: the x-axis marked from minus 2 to 2 and the y-axis from 0 to 3. The upward parabola f(x) = x squared has its lowest point at the dot at the origin, labelled f(0) = 0.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: f(x) = x² on (−∞, ∞) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example (c)
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = -x^{2} + 2\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
To find: its absolute extrema.
Method: compare \(f(x)\) with \(f(0)\) using \(-x^{2} \le 0\).

\[f(x) = 2 - x^{2} \le 2 = f(0)\]
So \(f\) has an absolute maximum value at \(x = 0\), where \(f(0) = 2\). (See Figure 2.4.)
Why: we always subtract a non-negative number \(x^{2}\) from 2.

It has no absolute minimum value.
Why: as \(x\) grows, \(-x^{2} + 2\) goes below every number (for example \(f(10) = -98\)).
blocks.answer: Absolute maximum value \(f(0) = 2\); no absolute minimum.

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel: the x-axis marked from minus 2 to 2 and the y-axis from 0 to 3. The downward parabola f(x) = minus x squared plus 2 has its highest point at the dot (0, 2), labelled f(0) = 2, and crosses the x-axis between 1 and 2 on each side.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4: f(x) = −x² + 2 on (−∞, ∞) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Compare (a) and (b): the same formula \(x^{2}\) has a global maximum on the closed interval \([0, 2]\) but none on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
A continuous function on a closed interval \([a, b]\) always has both a global maximum and a global minimum (the extreme value theorem). This is why 2.10.3 works on closed intervals.

rows: Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) has a local (relative) maxima at \(x = c \in I\), if there exists an open interval \(I_{1}\) such that \(c \in I_{1}\) and: \(f(c) \ge f(x)\) for all \(x \in I \cap I_{1}\).

Let \(I\) be an interval and let \(f: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. We say that \(f\) has a local (relative) minima at \(x = e \in I\), if there exists an open interval \(I_{1}\) such that \(e \in I_{1}\) and: \(f(e) \le f(x)\) for all \(x \in I \cap I_{1}\).
If \(f(x)\) has a local (relative) maximum at \(x = c\), then \(f(c)\) is called local (relative) maximum value of the function. (See Figure 2.5)
If \(f(x)\) has a local (relative) minimum at \(x = e\), then \(f(e)\) is called local (relative) minimum value of the function. (See Figure 2.5)

Labels: a, Absolute minimum (no smaller value of f anywhere, also a local minimum); c, Local maximum (no greater value of f nearby); e, Local minimum (no smaller value of f nearby); d, Absolute maximum (no greater value of f anywhere, also a local maximum); b, Local minimum. blocks.title: Teaching note
Teaching note
blocks.text: The open interval \(I_{1}\) in the definition is the "nearby" region; \(I \cap I_{1}\) keeps only the points that are also in the domain. That is why an end point such as \(a\) or \(b\) can be a local extremum: we compare it only with the points of \(I\) on one side.

rows: Compared with every \(x\) in the interval \(I\)
Compared only with \(x\) in a small open interval \(I_{1}\) around the point
At most one maximum value and one minimum value
There can be several local maxima and minima
May not exist either (for example a straight line)
Every global extremum is also a local one
A local extremum need not be global (c and e in Figure 2.5)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Global minimum at \(c\): \(f(c) \le f(x)\) for all \(x \in I\); global extrema = global maximum and minimum.
2. \(x^{2}\) on \([0, 2]\): max 4 at \(x = 2\), min 0 at \(x = 0\); on \((-\infty, \infty)\): min 0 at \(x = 0\), no max.
3. \(-x^{2} + 2\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\): max 2 at \(x = 0\), no min.
4. Local extrema compare a point only with nearby points; end points can be local extrema.
5. Every global extremum is also a local one, not conversely.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Saying \(x^{2}\) has a maximum on \((-\infty, \infty)\): it has none.
2. Calling the highest hill top in a small region the global maximum without comparing with the end points.
3. Forgetting that a local maximum can be lower than a local minimum elsewhere (compare the heights at \(c\) and \(b\) in Figure 2.5).
